theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: Before a job of terminating 20 outlets, why does a team leader check the tool kit against a list?
options: So every tool needed is there and safe to use
So the most costly tools can be left behind at the stores
So each trainee can bring their own tools
So the job can start before the plan is made

questions.stem: How can you tell that a screwdriver was made and tested as an insulated tool for electrical work?
options: Its handle is coloured red or yellow
It carries the double-triangle mark
It has a soft rubber grip on the handle
It was the dearest one in the shop

questions.stem: The insulation on the shaft of an insulated screwdriver has a deep cut. What should you do?
options: Wrap insulating tape round the cut
Use it only on 110 V circuits from now on
Take it out of use and replace it
Paint over the cut with clear varnish

questions.stem: Why must a neon tester screwdriver never be used to prove a circuit dead?
options: It always gives a reading that is too high
It can only be used on 220 V circuits
It needs a proving unit fitted inside it before each use
It can fail to light even when the circuit is live

questions.stem: Which tool should be used to prove a circuit dead before a cable is cut?
options: An approved two-pole voltage tester
A neon tester screwdriver
A continuity buzzer
A pair of insulated pliers

questions.stem: Before any hand tool is used on the conductors of a circuit, what must already be done?
options: The insulated tools must be warmed up
The circuit isolated, locked off and proved dead
The client must first sign the job card for the work
The cover plates must be cleaned

questions.stem: Why must the screwdriver tip fit the terminal screw head exactly?
options: So the screw can be turned with one finger
So the tool's insulation does not get warm
A poor fit slips, damages the head and leaves it loose
A tight fit lets you skip the torque check on each terminal

questions.stem: A flat-bladed screwdriver is used in a cross-head screw. What is most likely to happen?
options: The screw will tighten more quickly
The blade will lock into the screw
The screw will turn the other way
It slips and chews up the screw head

questions.stem: Why should ordinary side cutters not be used to cut steel wire or screws?
options: The hard steel notches or chips the blades
The cutters become magnetised
Steel wire cannot be cut by any hand tool
The handles lose their insulation

questions.stem: Which tool cuts a large cable, such as 35 mm², with a clean round end?
options: Small side cutters, in several bites
Ratchet or shear-type cable cutters
Long-nose pliers, twisted back and forth
A cable knife, sawn across the cable

questions.stem: Which is the safest way to cut a stiff 6 mm² conductor to length with cutters?
options: Let the waste end fly and sweep it up later
Cut it near your face so you can see the blades
Hold the waste end and point it away from people
Cut it while a team mate holds the far end tight

questions.stem: An automatic wire stripper starts to crush the copper of small conductors. What should you do?
options: Keep using it, as crushing does no harm
Use it only on the larger conductors from now on
Pull harder so that it strips more quickly
Adjust it, or take it out of use until fixed

questions.stem: A conductor is nicked while you strip it. What should you do?
options: Cut off the damaged part and strip again
Wrap the nick with tape and carry on
Use it, as a small nick does no harm
Solder over the nick to fill it in

questions.stem: When you remove the outer sheath of a cable with a knife, how deep should the cut be?
options: Right through, so the cores are cut too
Just through the sheath, not into the cores
Only a light scratch on the surface
As deep as the knife will go in one long pull

questions.stem: When you use a cable knife on a sheath, which way should the blade move?
options: Towards your thumb, for better control
Round and round the cable many times
Away from your body and hands, along the cable
Towards a team mate who is holding the cable steady

questions.stem: An insulated crimp terminal is coloured blue. About which conductor sizes is it usually made for? (Always check the maker's marking.)
options: About 0.5 to 1.5 mm²
About 4 to 6 mm²
About 10 to 16 mm²
About 1.5 to 2.5 mm²

questions.stem: Why does a ratchet crimping tool not open again until it has closed fully?
options: So every crimp gets the full pressure
So the tool cannot be lost
So the terminal can be removed later
So two crimps can be made at once

questions.stem: How should a finished crimp be checked?
options: Bend it back and forth until it is loose
Look at it, then give it a firm pull test
Heat it to see whether the barrel changes colour
Tap it with a hammer to settle the crimp

questions.stem: A 25 mm² cable needs a lug before it is bolted to a busbar. Which tool is right?
options: Pliers, squeezed very hard
A hammer and a centre punch
A lug crimper with the matching die
A small terminal crimper for red lugs

questions.stem: Your team must terminate 6 mm² stranded conductors into screw terminals. What should be fitted on the ends?
options: Solder, melted into each end
Insulating tape wound round the strands
Nothing; twist and fold the strands back
Ferrules, crimped with the right tool

questions.stem: Which pliers are best for forming a loop in a solid conductor for a screw terminal?
options: Round-nose or long-nose pliers
Large water pump pliers
Side cutters
Fencing pliers

questions.stem: Where no ferrule is used, why are the strands of a stranded conductor twisted together before going into a pillar terminal?
options: So the conductor looks neater from outside
So no loose strands stray out of the terminal
So the terminal screw does not need tightening
So the conductor size becomes larger

questions.stem: Your team must cut 40 lengths of 20 mm PVC conduit. Which choice gives square cuts quickly with the least waste?
options: Side cutters, worked round the conduit
A cable knife, rolled round the tube
A ratchet PVC conduit cutter
A pair of tin snips from the van

questions.stem: When sawing steel conduit by hand, why should at least three teeth of the blade be on the wall at once?
options: So the cut is finished in three strokes
So the blade never needs tensioning
So the conduit does not need a vice
So the teeth do not snag and break

questions.stem: After conduit is cut, why must the inside edge be reamed or filed smooth?
options: So burrs do not cut the cable insulation
So the conduit looks shiny when fitted
So the conduit becomes slightly longer
So the end can be painted more easily

questions.stem: Why is a knockout punch often chosen over drilling for a hole in a board that already holds equipment?
options: It works without any pilot hole at all
It cuts cleanly and leaves little swarf inside
It makes the hole any size you like
It does not need the board to be isolated first

questions.stem: Which tool should be used to tighten a cable gland's locknut inside a metal box?
options: Long-nose pliers
A flat screwdriver and hammer
A spanner or gland key of the right size
Side cutters

questions.stem: Which hand tools are used to cut a chase in a block wall?
options: A claw hammer and a wood chisel
A rubber mallet and a screwdriver
A ball pein hammer and a centre punch
A club hammer and a plugging chisel

questions.stem: The struck end of a chisel has spread out and cracked (mushroomed). Why is this dangerous?
options: Pieces can fly off when it is struck
It makes the chisel cut too deeply
It stops the chisel from rusting
It makes the chisel too light to use

questions.stem: A spirit level's bubble reads differently when it is turned end for end on the same surface. What does this show?
options: The surface is perfectly level
The level itself is out and needs checking
The bubble needs topping up with water
The level should only be used upside down from now on

questions.stem: A fish tape will not pass a bend in a conduit run. What is the best next step?
options: Force it harder until it goes through
Cut the conduit open at the bend
Try from the other end or a draw-in box
Pour engine oil into the conduit

questions.stem: Why must a steel fish tape never be pushed into a conduit or box that holds live cables?
options: It will stretch and lose its length
It could scratch the inside of the box
The cables might get tangled in it
It conducts and could touch live parts

questions.stem: Why should tools be counted before a board cover is put back on?
options: So no tool is left inside the board
So the client can see how many tools you own
So the cover fits more tightly
So the tools can be charged to the job

questions.stem: When you are on a ladder fixing a light fitting, where should your hand tools be kept?
options: On the top step of the ladder
In a tool belt or pouch on your waist
In your back pocket, points up
On the ceiling grid beside you

questions.stem: A trainee will strip and terminate about 200 conductors today. What helps most to prevent wrist strain?
options: Gripping the tools as hard as possible
Working without a break to finish early
Well-fitting tools with good grips, and breaks
Using one tool for every task, to save time changing

questions.stem: You see a trainee using pliers to tighten terminal screws. What should you do as team leader?
options: Leave him, as the screws are getting tight
Tell him to use the cutters instead
Finish the terminals yourself
Stop him and show the right screwdriver

questions.stem: A trainee strips insulation by biting it with side cutters and pulling. What is the main risk?
options: Nicked copper that can overheat or break
The insulation will come off too cleanly
The cutters will become too sharp
The conductor will get longer

questions.stem: How should the jaws and joints of pliers and cutters be cared for?
options: Soaked in water overnight to clean them
Wiped clean, joint lightly oiled, kept dry
Heated to burn off any dirt
Painted each month to stop rust

questions.stem: Why is a blunt cable knife more dangerous than a sharp one?
options: It cuts too deep into the cores
It is heavier to carry in a tool bag
It needs more force, so it is more likely to slip
It will rust much more quickly than a sharp one would

questions.stem: Which fault means a pair of insulated pliers must be taken out of use?
options: A little dust on the jaws
Writing worn off the handle
Slightly stiff joint after rain
Cracked or split handle insulation

questions.stem: Why are screwdrivers with a long, thin insulated shaft preferred for terminals deep inside a board?
options: They reach in while only the tip is bare metal
They turn screws faster than short ones
They can be used as a voltage tester
They let you work on the terminals without isolating

questions.stem: Why should cable ties not be cut with side cutters in a way that leaves a sharp tail?
options: The tie will come loose at once
The sharp tail can cut hands later
The cutters will be damaged by plastic
The cable will lose its insulation

questions.stem: A click-type torque screwdriver is set to 2.5 N·m. What happens when that torque is reached?
options: The blade locks so it cannot turn back
A light on the handle turns red
It clicks or slips, so you stop turning
The screw is pulled out of the terminal

questions.stem: Why does the Centre keep a register of its insulated tools with check dates?
options: To work out what to charge each trainee for using them
To decide which tools to sell first
To keep tools from being used at all
To show each one is inspected and fit for use

questions.stem: At the end of a job, what should the team do with the hand tools?
options: Clean, check, count and return them, reporting faults
Leave them in the van, ready for the next job on Monday
Put them all in one box to sort later
Give any damaged ones to a trainee to keep

essays.stem: You lead a team of four terminating a new distribution board and 12 circuits. Explain how you would plan, issue and control the hand tools for the job.
essays.modelAnswer: From the plan I would list the tasks: stripping sheaths, stripping and ferruling conductors, crimping lugs, glanding, terminating and labelling. For each task I list the tools, such as insulated screwdrivers of the right sizes, strippers, a sheath stripper, side cutters, a ferrule crimper, a lug crimper with the right dies, gland spanners and a torque screwdriver. I check the kit against the list, inspect each tool, especially the insulation on insulated tools, and replace any that are faulty. I issue tools by name on a sign-out sheet or shadow board, so I know who has what. During the job I watch that tools are used correctly. Before the cover goes on, the team counts every tool so none is left inside the board. At the end, tools are cleaned, checked, returned and faults reported.
markingPoints: Lists tasks and matching tools from the plan
Checks and inspects the kit, replacing faulty tools
Issues tools with a sign-out or shadow board
Supervises correct use during the job
Counts tools before closing the board; cleans, returns and reports

essays.stem: Explain how to inspect insulated hand tools before use, the faults to look for, and what to do with a faulty tool.
essays.modelAnswer: Before use I check that the tool is a proper insulated tool, marked with the double-triangle symbol and a 1000 V rating, and not just a tool with a plastic grip. I look along the whole insulation for cuts, cracks, splits, burns, holes or places where the insulation has worn through or slid along the shaft. I check that the insulation is firmly bonded and that the bare metal is limited to the working tip. I also check the working end: a screwdriver tip that is rounded or twisted, or cutter blades that are chipped, make the tool unsafe. A faulty insulated tool must not be taped or repaired, because the repair cannot be trusted. It is tagged, taken out of use, reported and recorded in the tool register, and replaced.
markingPoints: Checks for the insulated-tool mark and rating
Looks for cuts, cracks, burns and worn or loose insulation
Checks the working end (tip, jaws, blades)
Never tapes or repairs insulation
Tags, removes, reports, records and replaces

essays.stem: Describe how to prepare a sheathed multi-core cable and terminate it into screw terminals, naming each hand tool and saying how you avoid damage.
essays.modelAnswer: First the circuit is isolated, locked off, tagged and proved dead with a tester checked before and after. I measure the length of sheath to remove so the sheath enters the box or gland. I remove the sheath with a sheath stripper, or a cable knife cutting only through the sheath and away from my body, so the cores are not cut. I cut each core to length with side cutters, then set an adjustable wire stripper to the conductor size and strip just enough insulation for the terminal, using the strip gauge if there is one. On stranded conductors I crimp a ferrule of the right size with a ferrule crimper. I insert each core fully into its terminal with no bare copper showing and tighten with a screwdriver that fits the screw, to the maker's torque. Finally I give each core a gentle pull.
markingPoints: Safe isolation first, with tester checked before and after
Sheath removed without damaging the cores, blade away from body
Cores cut and stripped to the right length with set strippers
Ferrules crimped on stranded conductors
Correct screwdriver, torque, no bare copper, pull check

essays.stem: Explain how to choose and use crimp terminals and crimping tools, and how to check that a crimp is good.
essays.modelAnswer: I choose a terminal or lug that matches the conductor size and the stud or terminal it will go on. Insulated terminals are often colour coded, red for small, blue for medium and yellow for larger conductors, but I always check the maker's marking. I choose the crimping tool and die made for that terminal, so a ratchet crimper for small terminals and a lug crimper with the matching die for large lugs. I strip the conductor to the barrel length, insert it fully with no strands outside, and crimp in the right place, letting the ratchet complete its full cycle. Then I check the crimp by eye: the right die mark, no cracks, no bare strands and the conductor visible at the end of the barrel where the design allows. Finally I give it a firm pull test.
markingPoints: Terminal matched to conductor size and stud
Uses the matching tool and die (colour code checked against maker)
Correct strip length, conductor fully inserted
Full ratchet cycle, crimp in the right place
Visual check and pull test

essays.stem: Explain why safe isolation must come before any hand tool is used on a circuit, even with insulated tools, and describe the procedure, including the tester.
essays.modelAnswer: Insulated tools only give extra protection if something goes wrong; they do not make live work safe. A slip can bridge two conductors, causing a flash and burns, and a damaged tool or a bare tip can give a shock. So work is always done dead. I identify the right circuit, switch it off, and fit my own lock to the breaker or isolator with a lock-off device, so it cannot be switched on. I fix a tag with my name, the date and the reason. I check my approved voltage tester on a proving unit to show it works. Then I test between all the conductors and from each to earth at the point of work, to prove it is dead. I check the tester again on the proving unit. A neon screwdriver must never be used for this.
markingPoints: Insulated tools do not make live work safe; reasons
Identify, switch off and lock off with own lock
Tag with name, date and reason
Tester checked on a proving unit before and after
Test all conductors and to earth at the point of work; no neon screwdriver

essays.stem: Describe the hand tools and method for cutting and preparing steel and PVC conduit and fitting it to a box.
essays.modelAnswer: I mark the length with a tape and pencil or scriber. Steel conduit is held in a pipe vice and cut square with a hacksaw fitted with a fine blade, about 32 teeth per 25 mm, so at least three teeth are on the thin wall. PVC conduit can be cut with a ratchet conduit cutter or a fine hacksaw. After cutting, I ream the inside with a conduit reamer or half-round file and clean the outside, so no burr can cut the cables. Steel conduit is threaded with a die stock where the system needs threads. I fit the conduit to the box with the right coupler or bush, tightened with a spanner, pump pliers or the proper key, or for PVC with the right solvent cement as the maker says. Finally I check that the run is straight and secure and that every end is smooth.
markingPoints: Marks and holds the conduit properly
Correct saw blade or cutter, with reason
Reams and cleans every cut end
Threads steel conduit where needed
Fits to the box with the correct fittings and tools; checks the run

essays.stem: Describe how to cut a chase in a block wall by hand for a cable, including the tools, the safety precautions and making good.
essays.modelAnswer: First I check the plan and use a detector to make sure there are no cables or pipes in the wall where I will cut. I mark the chase with a level and pencil or a chalk line, running straight up or across from the box, not at an angle, so others can guess where the cable is. I wear safety glasses, gloves and a dust mask, and keep others clear of flying chips. I cut each edge with a bolster and club hammer, then remove the middle with a plugging chisel, keeping to the depth allowed so the wall is not weakened. I check that the chisels have no mushroomed heads. The cable or conduit is fixed in the chase and protected as required. Then the chase is filled with mortar or filler and made level with the wall, and the dust is cleaned up.
markingPoints: Checks for buried services before cutting
Marks a straight vertical or horizontal line
PPE and keeping others clear; chisel heads checked
Correct tools and depth
Fixes the cable, makes good and cleans up

essays.stem: Explain how to care for cutting and stripping tools, when to sharpen or replace them, and why damaged insulated tools must never be repaired.
essays.modelAnswer: After use I wipe cutters, strippers and knives clean and dry, oil the joints lightly and store them so their blades do not knock against other tools. A cable knife is kept sharp on a stone, because a blunt knife needs more force and slips. Strippers with replaceable blades get new blades when they start to tear the insulation instead of cutting it cleanly. Side cutters with chipped or notched jaws, or loose joints, are replaced, because they crush instead of cut. Crimpers are checked so the ratchet works and the dies are not worn. Insulated tools are never taped, glued or re-sleeved, because the repair has not been tested at the rated voltage and could fail without warning. Any damaged insulated tool is tagged, removed and replaced.
markingPoints: Clean, dry, oil joints and store safely
Keeps knives sharp; reason
Replaces worn blades, chipped cutters and loose joints
Checks crimper ratchet and dies
No repairs to insulated tools; reason and action

essays.stem: Describe four common misuses of hand tools in electrical work, the danger each causes, and how a team leader stops them happening.
essays.modelAnswer: One misuse is using pliers on terminal screws, which rounds the screws and leaves loose, hot connections. Another is stripping insulation with side cutters or a knife towards the hand, which nicks the copper and can cut the user. A third is using a neon screwdriver to check a circuit is dead, which can fail and lead to a shock. A fourth is using a damaged insulated tool or a screwdriver as a pry bar or chisel, which breaks the tool or its insulation. A team leader stops these by briefing the right tool for each task, making sure the right tools are in the kit, checking tools at the start of the day, watching the work and correcting misuse at once by showing the right way, and recording repeated problems so they can be dealt with.
markingPoints: Four realistic misuses named
The danger of each explained
Right tools supplied and briefed
Daily checks and close supervision
Correcting on the spot and recording repeat problems

essays.stem: Compare an adjustable wire stripper, an automatic wire stripper, a cable knife and a sheath stripper. Say when each is best and how to use each safely.
essays.modelAnswer: An adjustable wire stripper is set to the conductor size, so it is good for stripping single cores neatly without nicking them; I must set it correctly each time. An automatic stripper grips and strips in one squeeze, so it is quick for many conductors of mixed sizes; I check it is not crushing or nicking the copper. A cable knife is useful for large or unusual cables, but it is the most dangerous: I cut only through the sheath and always away from my body and hands, and keep it sharp. A sheath stripper has a guarded blade that cuts only the outer sheath, so it is best for removing sheaths quickly with little risk to the cores or the user. With all of them, the circuit is dead first and safety glasses are worn when cutting.
markingPoints: Adjustable stripper: use and setting
Automatic stripper: use and check for nicking
Cable knife: use, cutting away from the body, kept sharp
Sheath stripper: use and why it is safer
Circuit dead first and eye protection

practical1.title: Prepare, gland and terminate cables into a board and accessories using hand tools
practical1.brief: Working on a dead training board, the group terminates the cables for four circuits (for example a lighting circuit, an outlet circuit, a 220 V appliance circuit with stranded conductors and a submain with a crimped lug) into a small distribution board and two accessories. The group plans the tasks and lists the tools, inspects the kit, then isolates, locks off, tags and proves the training board dead with a tester checked before and after. Each member punches or fits one gland, strips one cable, and terminates at least one circuit, including either ferrules or a lug. Members check each other's terminations with a pull test and a torque screwdriver set to the assessor's value. Before the cover goes on, the group counts all tools. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical.
materials: Training board with lock-off point, and a small distribution board
Two accessories (outlet and switch) with boxes
Sheathed cables and stranded conductors as the assessor gives
Glands, ferrules and lugs to suit
Insulated screwdrivers, strippers, sheath stripper, side cutters, ferrule crimper, lug crimper
Knockout punch set and gland spanners
Torque screwdriver, voltage tester and proving unit, lock-off kit and tags
photos: The tool list and the inspected kit laid out
The board locked off and tagged, tester on the proving unit
A gland hole punched and the gland fitted
Stripped cores with ferrules and a crimped lug
Terminations inside the board before the cover goes on
The tool count before closing the board
checklist: Inspected their tools and rejected any faulty one
Followed safe isolation with a tester checked before and after
Removed the sheath and stripped cores without nicking copper
Crimped ferrules or a lug with the right tool and passed a pull test
Tightened terminals with a fitting screwdriver to the given torque
Used the knockout punch and gland tools correctly
Took part in the tool count and left the area clean
safety: Work only on the dead training board, locked off and tagged
Strip and cut away from the body and wear safety glasses
Use only insulated tools that pass inspection
Count tools before any cover is fitted

practical2.title: Inspect an electrician's tool kit, set up tool control, and make a conduit and box run
practical2.brief: Part A: the assessor gives the group a mixed kit of hand tools, some with planted faults (for example cut insulation, chipped cutters, a worn screwdriver tip, a crimper whose ratchet slips, a mushroomed chisel). As a group, inspect every tool, record the result on a tool register, tag the faulty ones, and set up a shadow board or tool roll with a sign-out sheet. Part B: using hand tools only, the group cuts, reams and fits a short run of steel or PVC conduit between two boxes on a training wall, with one bend set made using a hand bender if the Centre has one. Each member cuts and reams at least one length and fits at least one fitting. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical.
materials: Mixed hand tool kit with planted faults
Tool register, faulty tags and sign-out sheet
Steel or PVC conduit, couplers, boxes and saddles
Hacksaw with fine blade, PVC conduit cutter, reamer and half-round file
Pipe vice, tape, level and pencil
Hand bender (if the Centre has one)
photos: The kit laid out for inspection
The faulty tools tagged, with the register filled in
The shadow board or tool roll with the sign-out sheet
A conduit length being cut in the vice
A reamed conduit end, close up
The finished conduit run between the boxes
checklist: Found and recorded the planted faults correctly
Tagged faulty tools and did not use them
Helped set up the tool control system
Cut conduit square with the right blade or cutter
Fitted the run level and secure with the right fittings and tools
Returned tools clean and signed them back in
safety: Hold conduit in a vice when sawing; keep hands clear of the blade
Wear safety glasses and gloves when cutting and reaming
Do not use any tool tagged as faulty
Keep the work area clear of offcuts
